https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world.text: Germany faces daily hybrid warfare attacks from abroad, interior minister Alexander Dobrindt was quoted as saying on Sunday, following a suspected attack attempt involving an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport. Dobrindt told the newspaper Bild am Sonntag that foreign powers wanted to subdue Germany politically and socially by stirring up fear there. Dobrindt highlighted the expansion ‌of drone ​research in Germany as part ‌of the response to the ​new threats. “We're not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare,” Dobrindt said. “Espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks, or covert operations by foreign powers aimed at destabilising Germany or inflicting direct harm are a constant reality.” The newspaper's advance ​release ⁠of the interview did ‌not say whether he identified any countries in particular. After the drone loaded with explosives was discovered at the airport in eastern Germany on Tuesday, some German lawmakers pointed the finger at Russia, which has been at war with Ukraine since its military invasion of the country in 2022. The Russian embassy in Berlin on Friday dismissed the Leipzig event as a "fabricated provocation", saying it was another example of accusations against Russia without evidence.

https://www.dailysabah.com/world/europe/.text: World Mid-East Europe Americas Asia Pacific Africa Syrian Crisis Islamophobia Zelenskyy says US briefed Ukraine on recent Moscow meetings by Reuters Aug 28, 2026 - 9:58 pm GMT+3 Edited By Nurbanu Tanrıkulu Kızıl Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks during a press conference with Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic (not pictured) following their meeting in Belgrade, Serbia, Aug. 8, 2026. (EPA File Photo) by Reuters Aug 28, 2026 9:58 pm Edited By Nurbanu Tanrıkulu Kızıl Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday that Washington had shared intelligence with Kyiv about a series of meetings held in Moscow in recent days. "Today we ⁠received information from the American side about the meetings in Moscow that took place these days. There ​were a number of meetings there," Zelenskyy said ​on ⁠Telegram, without going into detail on who was at the meetings. "I thank them for the information and for the necessary tone of the conversation with Russia," Zelenskyy added, again without elaborating. The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that CIA Director John Ratcliffe had travelled to Moscow to warn Russia off any attack on a NATO member. The Kremlin dismissed the report, while U.S. President Donald Trump said Russian President Vladimir Putin would not attack a ⁠NATO ⁠country, playing down media reports on Ratcliffe's trip. Two sources told Reuters that Ratcliffe had raised the possibility of a Russian operation against a NATO member during the meeting, although it was unclear whether that was the primary purpose of the trip. The talks also covered Russia's support for Iran, one source told Reuters. Also Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on ⁠Friday that Warsaw was in constant contact with the CIA leadership and was not surprised byRatcliffe's visit to Moscow. "We are not taken by surprise by ​any information regarding the operations and initiatives the CIA Director is conducting," Tusk ​told a youth conference when asked if the visit should be a source of concern. "Poland was also informed ⁠about ‌the need ‌for an urgent discussion on this matter at ⁠the highest possible Polish-American level," Tusk ‌added without elaborating. He said that there have been signals in the public ​domain that Russia is preparing ⁠to escalate tensions, both in the war with ⁠Ukraine and across the region, and that this autumn ⁠and winter are set ​to be pivotal for Russia. shortlink copied KEYWORDS russia-ukraine war volodymyr zelenskyy The Daily Sabah Newsletter Keep up to date with what’s happening in Turkey, it’s region and the world. https://www.dw.com/en/pakistan-president.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5O83e Pakistan's government has been bracing for the arrival of Imran Khan supporters demanding the former PM be released from prison Image: REUTERS Advertisement Pakistan's President Asif Ali Zardari on Sunday announced that the northwestern Pakistani province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had been put under emergency rule, effectively removing power from former Prime Minster Imran Khan 's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party. The imposition of emergency rule comes as thousands of Khan supporters continue to stage anti-government protests and demand the former leader be released from jail . Current Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif proposed the move, which Zardari signed into order on Sunday. The suspension of regional government was justified under constitutional articles that allow the central government to confront security threats and give it sweeping powers in emergency situations. Sharif's government claims regional authorities have not done enough to curb Islamist violence in the province. Authorities have set up massive roadblocks across Pakistan to keep Khan supporters at bay Image: Abdul Majeed/AFP Why is Pakistan's government taking control of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa? Last Sunday, thousands of Khan's supporters began to make their way from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to the Pakistani capital, Islamabad. Organizers had declared their intent to rally hundreds of thousands more along the way in hopes of bringing about Khan's release from prison. Despite being jailed since 2023, Khan, a popular former cricket star, maintains great influence in Pakistan, with he and his followers convinced that his imprisonment is the result of political persecution. Khan, who began his term as prime minister in August 2018, was ousted from office in April 2022 after losing a no-confidence vote. Khan's supporters want him released from jail Image: Faridullah Khan/DW He has been in prison since August 2023. Beyond corruption and treason charges, he was also accused of inciting violence after widespread anti-government protests in May 2023. Khan rejects the charges as a politically motivated plot to keep him away from power. He remains a popular political figure in Pakistan. Khan's supporters claim that the 2024 election that brought Shehbaz Sharif back to power was rigged — an accusation the government denies. Pakistan has seen a resurgence of terror attacks over the past several months and the Sharif government accuses Khan's PTI of sympathizing with the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, which is largely thought to be behind the attacks. The PTI rejects these accusations as a baseless smear campaign. https://www.politico.eu/article/poland-h.text: WARSAW — Poland wants domestic companies to supply more of its rapidly expanding military, but state-owned PGZ’s fragmented structure and political exposure raise questions about whether Warsaw can turn the spending surge into a stronger industry. The Polish Armaments Group, the country’s largest defense company, has won billions of złoty in new orders, placing it at the center of the military buildup. The conglomerate was cobbled together in 2013 from about 50 fiercely independent smaller companies with their own management teams and often their own political backers. CEO Adam Leszkiewicz has been in the post since May 2025 — making him the holding company's 12th CEO since its founding. Advertisement Advertisement "PGZ is different from other European companies,” Leszkiewicz said, adding that PGZ makes more than 700 products. "I could say we make almost everything. But what can be a strength can also be a weakness.” Marek Świerczyński, a defense analyst with the Warsaw-based Polityka Insight Center for Policy Analysis, said: “He essentially has to use diplomacy to try to manage the other companies.” Legacy defense industry For decades after the end of communism, Poland spent little on defense and the military largely made do with antiquated Soviet-era equipment. Russia’s illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014 and its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 changed that, and Polish defense spending surged. “We have strong historical and current experience with armored vehicles and maintenance, repair and overhaul services,” said Leszkiewicz. “We also make wheeled vehicles such as the Jelcz, and our work on sensors and radar is developing well. We have long been strong in rifles and pistols.” Aleksandra Kozioł, a defense analyst with the Warsaw-based Polish Institute of International Affairs, pointed out other notable Polish defense companies, such as the private WB Group, which specializes in communications networks, unmanned aerial vehicles, loitering munitions and fire control solutions. “We want to improve in new technologies, especially unmanned vehicles as well as software and IT solutions,” Leszkiewicz said. Advertisement Advertisement PGZ is also building ties with other European defense firms. It is building three new artillery shell factories in conjunction with the U.K.'s BAE Systems . PGZ's Narew air defense system includes a tie-up with MBDA to supply missiles and launchers. “Either we take advantage of this opportunity, or we let this period of rapid industrial development in defense pass. We have ambitions and want to fulfill them,” Leszkiewicz said. Keeping the cash at home This year, Poland aims to spend 200 billion złoty (€45.7 billion) — or 4.8% of GDP — on defense, the highest level in NATO. It is also the largest recipient of the EU’s €150 billion SAFE loans-for-arms program , taking in almost €44 billion. The government is trying to ensure that the country’s defense industry gets a growing share of the new spending. In May, Poland's Armaments Agency signed almost 120 billion złoty in contracts with Polish arms companies financed by SAFE. A large share went to PGZ and its subsidiaries, mainly Huta Stalowa Wola, for equipment including 146 Borsuk infantry fighting vehicles, 96 Krab howitzers, 64 Rak mortars, K9PL support vehicles and 1,000 vehicles for the Homar-K rocket-launcher system. Most of the deals with PGZ were no-bid contracts, according to a report by the Warsaw Enterprise Institute think tank. Advertisement Advertisement "The development of the Polish defense industry is necessary, but it should not automatically mean preferential treatment for companies directly controlled by the government," the report said. Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz last month underlined that the government aims to develop the country's military-industrial complex, saying: “We are building a strong army, strengthening security, and investing in Poland's future.” But favoring domestic companies risks clashing with the government's drive to rearm as quickly as possible; Warsaw wants to buy tanks, jets and missiles to deter Russia, although that goal does pose problems for its domestic arms industry. A drone hangs above visitors' heads at the WB Group stand at the International Defence Industry Exhibition in Kielce, Poland on Sept. 8, 2026. | Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images About 60 percent of Poland’s defense spending goes on imports, “and that won’t change quickly,” said Świerczyński. Most arms imports come from South Korea and the United States, including systems like K2 Black Panther tanks and F-35A fighter jets. “In 2022, we were looking for ready-made solutions and products because we felt threatened,” said Leszkiewicz. “Today, we are trying to take every opportunity to Polonize production. We are now hardly buying ready-made products, except where we really lack a particular capability.” One of PGZ's subsidiaries will be building K2 tanks starting in 2028. "I do see an effort to increase Polish intellectual property," said Kozioł, the defense analyst, adding that it's still unclear if the government's effort to shift contracts to Polish firms will lessen the reliance on foreign technology. Advertisement Advertisement In 2025, PGZ reported 18.4 billion złoty in revenues, a 23% increase on the previous year, and 2.8 billion złoty in profit, a 66% increase. The company ranked 51st in the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute's 2025 list of the world's top 100 defense companies. "We aim to reach the top 10 in Europe and the top 30 globally," said Leszkiewicz. "If we look at PGZ's development and results, it appears that, despite political issues, the company is trying to fulfill the task of arming the Polish military," said Kozioł. Political risk Polish state-controlled companies are notorious for high levels of political interference. Although Kozioł underlined that there is a cross-party consensus in favor of continued high defense spending, PGZ does face political risks. Mateusz Morawiecki, prime minister from 2017 to 2023 under the previous Law and Justice Party government, this summer called for PGZ to potentially be dissolved, accusing it of “weak” management. Kosiniak-Kamysz fired back, calling the idea “harmful and anti-state.” Advertisement Advertisement The danger is likely to grow. Poland holds a parliamentary election next year and opinion polls suggest that Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s coalition could be unseated by a grouping of right-wing parties. That means Leszkiewicz's position — he was a junior member of Tusk’s previous government from 2007 to 2011 and took over PGZ after running state-controlled fertilizer giant Grupa Azoty — could be under threat. “A CEO would have to be in the job for a decade, but in Polish realities there is no chance of that,” said Świerczyński.
